title: The Biggest Risk in Agentic AI Is Not the Model, It’s the System Around It
summary: Why agentic AI in banking is first and foremost a governance problem.
body_markdown:
Banks are moving quickly towards agentic AI. The logic is easy to understand. Instead of relying on a single model to complete a task, institutions can orchestrate multiple specialised models and tools together. One agent retrieves data, another analyses it, another drafts a recommendation, another checks compliance.


On paper, this looks like the next phase of AI maturity. In practice, it introduces a very different category of risk.


Most conversations around agentic AI still focus on capability. How autonomous should agents become? Which models perform best? How much productivity can be unlocked? Those are not the questions banks should be prioritising first.


Because the challenge with orchestration is not whether the individual models work. It is whether the overall system remains understandable, governable, and controllable once those models begin interacting with each other at scale.


And that problem becomes significantly harder in banking environments, where decisions carry regulatory, financial, and operational consequences.


## A single model creates decision risk. Orchestrated agents create systems risk.


A single model is relatively straightforward to govern. Inputs are defined. Outputs are monitored. Lineage can usually be traced. If something goes wrong, the scope of investigation is contained.


Agentic systems change those conditions completely. Now multiple models interact dynamically. Outputs from one process become inputs into another. Decisions are passed between agents, often with varying levels of autonomy and context. In some cases, external tools or APIs are introduced into the chain as well.


The complexity is no longer additive. It becomes compounding. A customer servicing workflow is a useful example. One agent retrieves customer history, another summarises recent interactions, another proposes a next-best action, and another checks whether the recommendation falls within policy constraints.


Individually, each component may perform well. The problem emerges in the interaction between them. A small inconsistency introduced upstream can propagate through the chain in ways that are difficult to detect. A recommendation may technically comply with policy while still being based on incomplete context. An escalation path may fail because one agent interprets confidence differently from another.


In orchestrated systems, small upstream failures rarely stay isolated. While at small scale, these issues may appear manageable, at production scale, they become systemic.


## The audit trail starts disappearing the moment agents start interacting


One of the more uncomfortable realities of orchestration is that explainability becomes harder precisely as institutions become more dependent on AI-driven decisions. In traditional systems, auditability is already difficult. In agentic systems, it can deteriorate quickly.


Not because banks stop capturing information, but because the volume and interconnectedness of decisions become difficult to reconstruct in any meaningful way.


Which agent made the recommendation? Which model influenced the outcome? Which version of the prompt was used? What external data was retrieved at the time? What sequence of interactions led to the final decision? These are no longer edge-case questions. They become operational requirements.


And in many current architectures, the answers are fragmented across logs, platforms, orchestration layers, and model providers. This creates a dangerous illusion of control. Institutions can see individual components operating, but struggle to explain how the system behaved as a whole.


The more agents a bank introduces, the less obvious it becomes who is actually making the decision. That distinction matters more than most organisations currently appreciate.


Regulators are unlikely to accept “the orchestration layer was too complex to reconstruct” as an explanation for a failed decision, particularly in regulated processes involving lending, fraud, financial crime, or customer outcomes.


The more autonomous systems become, the more important traceability becomes alongside them.


## Most AI governance models were designed for a world before orchestration


Governance structures in banking were largely built around relatively stable systems. Model validation happens periodically. Risk reviews follow defined approval cycles. Ownership boundaries are clear.


Agentic systems do not behave that way. They evolve continuously. Prompts change. Dependencies shift. Models are updated. Agents begin interacting with new data sources and tools over time.


That creates a governance mismatch. A system that changes dynamically cannot be governed effectively through static oversight processes alone.


This is where many institutions risk underestimating the scale of organisational change required. The challenge is not simply introducing new controls. It is redesigning how accountability operates when decisions are distributed across interconnected agents rather than contained within individual applications.


Even basic ownership questions become harder to answer. Who is responsible when an orchestrated process fails? The model team? The platform team? The data owner? The business function that deployed the workflow?


In many organisations, the answer is still unclear. That ambiguity may be manageable in experimentation phases. It becomes much more serious once these systems are embedded into core banking operations.


## The hidden cost of orchestration is operational overhead


There is also a commercial reality that receives far less attention than it should.


Agentic architectures can become extremely expensive to operate if orchestration is not carefully controlled.


Each interaction between agents carries compute, inference, storage, monitoring, governance, and coordination overhead. As workflows become more sophisticated, those costs multiply quickly.


The issue is not simply model cost. It is system cost. A process involving six interconnected agents may generate significantly more operational overhead than a single-model workflow, particularly when observability, auditability, failover controls, and human review layers are added.


This matters because many current AI business cases are still built around isolated model economics rather than end-to-end operational behaviour. At pilot scale, the gap is often hidden. At enterprise scale, it becomes very visible. Institutions that do not establish cost discipline early risk building orchestration layers that are technically impressive but commercially difficult to sustain.


## The banks that scale agentic AI successfully will approach it differently


The institutions that succeed here are unlikely to be the ones deploying the highest number of agents the fastest. They will be the banks that treat orchestration as a systems engineering and governance challenge first, and an AI capability effort second.


That changes the priorities significantly. It means designing traceability into workflows before autonomy increases. It means reducing unnecessary architectural fragmentation before introducing orchestration layers on top. It also means establishing clear ownership models for agent behaviour, escalation, and accountability, and resisting the temptation to treat orchestration as purely a tooling problem.


The underlying issue is structural. Agentic AI increases the number of interconnected decisions inside the organisation. If the surrounding data, governance, and operational foundations are weak, orchestration amplifies those weaknesses rather than solving them.


This is why some of the most important investments in agentic AI will not look like AI investments at all. They will look like work on architecture, lineage, observability, governance, and operational resilience.


## The orchestration layer is becoming part of the control environment


Over the next decade, orchestration will likely become one of the defining layers of enterprise AI architecture in banking. Not because orchestrated systems are inherently risky, but because they fundamentally change how decisions are produced, coordinated, and controlled across the organisation.


That makes orchestration more than a technical capability. It becomes part of the bank’s operational control environment.


And in the next phase of banking AI, the institutions that succeed will not be the ones with the highest number of agents or the fastest deployment cycles. They will be the ones that can still explain, govern, and control their systems after thousands of autonomous decisions begin interacting at scale.
